prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat with corticosteroids: oral corticosteroids are strongly advised against and IV methylprednisolone is not recommended [EAN_PNS_2023].
Do not give IVIg directly after plasma exchange, and do not give a second IVIg course [EAN_PNS_2023, Walgaard_2021].
Do not start IVIg without checking renal function.
Do not use succinylcholine if intubation is needed: denervated muscle risks severe hyperkalaemia.
Do not attribute the acute syndrome to the known diabetic neuropathy without evaluating for GBS.
required_recommendations: Admit to a monitored high-dependency bed with FVC, MIP and MEP every 4 to 6 hours and checks of bulbar function, cough and secretions; move to ICU-level care if FVC falls below 60% predicted or 20 mL/kg (about 1.45 L at 72.3 kg) or by more than 30%, MIP becomes weaker than -40 cmH2O, MEP falls below 40 cmH2O, or cough weakens or secretions pool [Lawn_2001, EAN_PNS_2023].

Start IVIg 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total, about 29 g/day at 72.3 kg) or plasma exchange 200-250 mL/kg over 5 sessions: he cannot walk unaided and is 10 days from onset; check renal function and keep him well hydrated during IVIg [EAN_PNS_2023].
Continuous cardiac telemetry with blood pressure monitoring for autonomic instability while weakness progresses.
Formal swallow assessment before oral intake (dysphagia for solids, diminished gag, dysarthria); modify diet or keep nil by mouth until assessed.
Monitor blood glucose during the acute illness; hold metformin if oral intake stops or renal function falls, and use insulin as needed.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Functional / metabolic brain imaging adds no value in a peripheral demyelinating syndrome.
Cerebrovascular imaging is not indicated in a peripheral neuropathy without focal cerebral signs.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AIDP superimposed on pre-existing diabetic peripheral neuropathy

differential.diagnosis: Acute worsening of diabetic polyneuropathy / diabetic amyotrophy
differential.key_features: Excluded as the cause: acute four-limb weakness with global areflexia, facial and bulbar weakness, CSF albuminocytological dissociation and demyelinating conduction slowing with absent F-waves are not features of diabetic polyneuropathy; diabetic amyotrophy is asymmetric, painful and proximal in the legs.
Cannot be excluded at presentation: a 10-day course fits GBS; reconsider if progression continues beyond 8 weeks or treatment-related fluctuations recur.
No tick exposure reported; CSF has no pleocytosis, whereas Lyme radiculitis gives a lymphocytic pleocytosis.
Glucose 142 mg/dL with a normal bicarbonate: no metabolic decompensation, and it would not explain acute areflexia and demyelinating NCS.
Symmetric not multifocal; no systemic features.

key_clinical_evidence: Baseline diabetic neuropathy raises the bar for diagnosing GBS: the anchor is acute symmetric four-limb weakness with global areflexia and facial weakness after an upper respiratory infection, with CSF albuminocytological dissociation and a demyelinating NCS (Brighton level 1) [Brighton_2011].
EMG demyelinating features that exceed expected diabetic chronic neuropathy support superimposed AIDP.

Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL allows IVIg; diabetes adds to the risk of IVIg-related kidney injury, so hydrate and recheck creatinine during the course; plasma exchange is the alternative if renal function falls.
Glucose rises with acute illness: monitor it and adjust diabetes treatment, including metformin if intake or renal function falls.
The antecedent infection is a history finding; serology is not needed for the diagnosis, and a positive IgM does not prove the trigger.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Diabetic neuropathy is chronic and length-dependent; acute symmetric areflexia with rapid progression and elevated CSF protein indicates a new GBS process.
red_herrings.data_point: Known diabetic peripheral neuropathy, diagnosed 2 years ago
red_herrings.intended_effect: Lead the clinician to attribute all neurological signs to diabetic neuropathy and miss the superimposed GBS.

interactions: Metformin with intravenous immunoglobulin: no direct interaction; IVIg can cause acute kidney injury, which raises the risk of metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis; relative caution, monitor creatinine.
Metformin with plasma exchange: no clinically significant interaction.
general.summary: Current medication reviewed: metformin 500 mg twice daily.
warnings: Hold metformin if eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 or oral intake stops.

ecg.interpretation: Sinus tachycardia, rate 104. Borderline QTc prolongation (452 ms). No acute ST-T wave changes.

labs.interpretation: Glucose 142 mg/dL (elevated). HbA1c 7.2% (elevated). CRP 16.1 mg/L and ESR 38 mm/hr (elevated). Blood count, renal function, electrolytes, liver tests, albumin and CK within normal limits. HIV non-reactive.

results.finding: Guidelines for adults with GBS who cannot walk unaided advise IVIg 2 g/kg over 5 days within 2 weeks of onset or plasma exchange within 4 weeks, with no preference between them; corticosteroids are not advised.
A second IVIg course in patients with a poor predicted prognosis did not improve outcome and caused more serious adverse events.

general.summary: IVIg or plasma exchange is advised for adults with GBS unable to walk unaided; neither is preferred, and a second IVIg course is not advised [EAN_PNS_2023, Walgaard_2021].

findings.finding: DML 6.1 ms (prolonged; normal <4.2 ms); CV 40 m/s (reduced; normal >49 m/s); CMAP 3.8 mV (mildly reduced; normal >4.0 mV)
DML 8.8 ms (prolonged; normal <6.0 ms); CV 30 m/s (reduced; normal >41 m/s)
Absent in bilateral peroneal; prolonged (>60 ms) in bilateral median
Reduced recruitment of normal-morphology motor unit potentials in tibialis anterior and vastus lateralis bilaterally; no fibrillation potentials or positive sharp waves

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL nerve conduction study and needle EMG. 1. Prolonged distal motor latencies and reduced conduction velocities in bilateral median and peroneal motor nerves. 2. Absent sural SNAPs bilaterally; reduced median sensory amplitudes. 3. Absent F-waves in bilateral peroneal nerves; prolonged F-wave latencies (>60 ms) in bilateral median nerves. 4. Absent H-reflex bilaterally. 5. Reduced recruitment without active denervation on needle EMG. Findings indicate a demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.

quantitative_data.proximal_involvement: Absent peroneal and prolonged median F-waves

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required actions, 1 red herring; GBS on a background of diabetic neuropathy, which must not absorb the acute syndrome.
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 GBS audit: spine MRI is optional and limited to five cases with a concrete cord, traumatic, postoperative or infiltrative alternative; generic hidden MRI reports removed.

patient.chief_complaint: Ten-day rapidly progressive leg weakness and paresthesias with areflexia in a diabetic man, preceded by respiratory illness.

past_medical_history: Mild peripheral neuropathy diagnosed 2 years ago, attributed to diabetes

social_history.tobacco: Former smoker, 20 pack-years, quit 8 years ago

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. G. is a 58-year-old man with known mild diabetic peripheral neuropathy presenting with a 10-day history of rapidly worsening leg weakness. Three weeks before presentation, he had a 5-day upper respiratory illness. About 6 days after it resolved, he noticed new bilateral foot numbness more severe than his usual diabetic neuropathy. Over the following week, weakness rapidly progressed: he went from difficulty with stairs to being unable to walk without bilateral support. He noticed bilateral facial drooping when shaving. He has difficulty swallowing solids over the past 3 days. He denies respiratory distress at rest. His wife noted that his new symptoms are distinctly different from his usual diabetic foot tingling; she says he could previously walk normally. His neurologist saw him 3 months ago for diabetic neuropathy and noted only trace foot vibration loss; no weakness at that time.

neurological_exam.additional: Respiratory: breathing comfortably at rest, no accessory muscle use. Cough effective.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral mild facial weakness — forehead sparing absent (lower face predominantly but forehead mildly involved). No ptosis. Gag reflex diminished. Dysarthria mild.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented. Frustrated and scared.
neurological_exam.motor: Moderate bilateral lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 3+/5, knee extension 4/5, ankle dorsiflexion 3/5. Upper extremities: 4/5 throughout.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Global areflexia — absent bilaterally at all tendon reflexes.
neurological_exam.sensory: Bilateral distal paresthesias. Reduced pinprick and vibration in stocking distribution to mid-calf bilaterally.
